meta.tagline: Two banks of the Danube, thermal steam and the city of ruin bars

pills: A UNESCO night view over the Danube
Where the ruin bar was born

overview.title: Welcome to Budapest
overview.intro: Budapest is really two cities, and the Danube makes both jealous: the Buda side is stately with its hills, castle and quiet lanes; the Pest side wild with its boulevards, coffeehouses and ruin bars. Beneath it all bubble more than a hundred thermal springs — this city has healed with water and socialised in steam for centuries. When evening comes, the Parliament burns like a golden jewel and the Chain Bridge ties the two banks together with a necklace of light. Budapest is a city of domes by day and of water by night.

local_word.definition: 'Ruin bar': the Budapest invention of bars built into the courtyards of abandoned buildings, full of old armchairs and odd objects. The first opened in the early 2000s — today it is the city's night-time identity itself.

rules.title: Enter the baths properly
rules.description: The thermal pools are not swimming pools: in 38-degree water you don't race, you converse — some even play chess. Read the slipper and cap rules at the entrance and start the hot-cold-sauna cycle slowly. Stay at least two hours; hurry is the enemy of steam.

rules.title: Never hail a taxi off the street
rules.description: In Budapest a trustworthy taxi comes when called: by app or official dispatcher. A car flagged on the street may run on the tourist tariff. Public transport is excellent anyway — metro line 1 is a historic monument in itself.

rules.title: Put the night view on the schedule
rules.description: Budapest's UNESCO panorama opens at night: Parliament, castle and bridges turn to gold in the dark. Devote one evening to the water — a boat, a riverside walk or Gellért Hill; whichever it is, wait for darkness.

quick_facts.label: Getting around
quick_facts.sub: M1 is continental Europe's oldest metro

tip.label: The Budapest philosophy
tip.text: In this city the day splits in two: history on Buda's hills by day, life in Pest's courtyards by night. Cross the Danube at least twice a day — every bridge shows a different city.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Budapest's transport is both efficient and nostalgic: a century-old metro, yellow trams, and along the Danube one of the world's most scenic tram lines.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: The 100E express bus runs straight to the centre — buy its special ticket at the machine. Taxis are safe from the official rank at a fixed tariff, and the ride apps work smoothly too.

items.title: M1 — a little yellow piece of history
items.description: The Millennium metro of 1896 runs beneath Andrássy Avenue with its tiny porcelain-tiled stations: it is a sight in its own right. M2, M3 and M4 complete the modern network.

items.title: Tram 2 — a box seat on the Danube
items.description: Line 2 along the Pest embankment counts among the world's most scenic tram rides: Parliament, the bridges and the Buda skyline pass your window. A world tour on a standard ticket.

items.title: On foot, bank by bank
items.description: Central Pest is flat and walkable; the Buda side is hilly — for the castle take the funicular from Clark Ádám Square or bus 16. Crossing the bridges on foot is the programme itself.

items.title: MOL Bubi and the embankment paths
items.description: The shared green bikes are the short hop's friend: Margaret Island's car-free roads and the riverside lanes might as well have been built for pedalling.

callout.label: Tram tip
callout.text: Ride tram 2 after dark: gliding along the embankment while Parliament blazes is the ticket-price version of the paid night cruises. Do the same line once more by day — you'll see two different cities.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: Choosing a bank is choosing a soul: in Pest you sleep inside the life, in Buda above the view.

local_word.definition: The coffeehouse: the gilded salons that were the tables of writers and revolutions in 1900s Budapest. They are still open — with a coffee and a slice of torte at a marble table, you are beamed back to that age.

items.name: District V — Belváros
items.description: The elegant centre between Parliament, the basilica and the embankment: walk everywhere, a kávéház on every corner. Prices above the city average but the location flawless — the classic for a first visit.

items.name: District VII — the Jewish Quarter
items.description: The quarter of ruin bars, synagogues and street food: sleepless, wall-painted, layered with history. Light sleepers should ask for a courtyard room — the street side is alive till dawn.

items.name: Buda — the Castle and Víziváros
items.description: The stone lanes of Castle Hill and Víziváros between hill and river: the castle is yours before the tourists arrive, and Pest's lights lie at your feet at night. Calm and stately.

items.name: District IX — around Ráday street
items.description: The restaurant street Ráday and the market hall's neighbourhood: two stops to the centre, prices a notch friendlier, terraces at night. Where local life crosses the tourist route.

items.name: District XIII — Újlipótváros
items.description: A calm quarter of Bauhaus apartment houses next to Margaret Island: coffee roasters, neighbourhood restaurants and riverside running paths. Low on tourists, high on quality of life.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Budapest works in all four seasons: spring means terraces, summer festivals, autumn new wine, winter steaming pools and Christmas lights.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Terrace Season
items.subtitle: Spring · Open-air beginnings, the Spring Festival
items.description: The kávéház tables move onto the pavements, Margaret Island turns green and the Spring Festival fills the city with concerts. In the baths' outdoor pools, the cool air + hot water balance is exactly right.

callout.label: May tip
callout.text: In May climb Gellért Hill before sunset: in spring light the Danube turns silver, and when darkness falls the Parliament is plated in gold. One climb, two views.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Festival and Island
items.subtitle: Summer · Sziget festival, open-air cinema, hot days
items.description: In August the Sziget Festival turns Óbuda island into a week-long republic; in the city the open-air bars and embankment evenings stretch long. On hot days the remedy is fixed: a bath's pool or Margaret Island's fountains.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: On the 20 August national holiday one of Europe's biggest fireworks displays goes up over the Danube: the embankments fill early and the bridges close. Claim your spot in the late afternoon and plan to walk home.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Golden Boulevard
items.subtitle: Autumn · Chestnut-coloured avenues, new wine
items.description: Andrássy's trees turn gold, wine festivals set up in the castle courtyard and the kávéház season warms. The crowds thin — this is the season of photographs and museums.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: If you coincide with the wine festival at Buda Castle in September, don't miss it: all of Hungary's vineyards in one courtyard, the Danube view behind you. Start with Tokaji, continue with kékfrankos.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Steam and Light
items.subtitle: Winter · Christmas markets, steaming outdoor pools
items.description: The Christmas market glows before the basilica and Vörösmarty Square fills with huts; the real magic is the outdoor thermal pools steaming in sub-zero air. If it snows, your hair freezes and your shoulders simmer in Széchenyi's pool — the signature frame of a Budapest winter.

callout.label: December tip
callout.text: On a winter morning reach Széchenyi at opening: steam columns rising, the pool calm, the light golden. Approach the chess-playing gentlemen's board — watching is allowed, respect is required.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Hungarian cooking is generous and red: paprika is every pot's soul, gulyás a national treasure, the desserts an imperial inheritance.

local_word.definition: Hungary's red gold: dozens of varieties from sweet to hot form the kitchen's foundation. The ground pepper of the Kalocsa and Szeged regions is national pride — for a gift, buy it upstairs at the market, in a linen bag.

items.name: Gulyás — the national pot
items.description: Goulash here is a soup, not a stew: paprika beef with potatoes and csipetke dumplings. If you find it cooked in a cauldron, you're lucky — dunking bread is the custom.
items.tag: National classic · look for the cauldron

items.name: Lángos — the street legend
items.description: Fried dough painted with garlic water, sour cream and grated cheese: the official meal of the market hall and the lido. Eaten by hand; one napkin will not suffice, and there are no regrets.
items.tag: At a market stall · the garlicky classic

items.name: Paprikás csirke and főzelék
items.description: Chicken in creamy paprika sauce with galuska dumplings: the heart of the Sunday table. Főzelék (thick vegetable purée) is Budapest's humble lunch tradition — try it like a local.

items.name: Kávéház desserts — Dobos and Eszterházy
items.description: The caramel-topped Dobos torte and the walnut Eszterházy: century-old window classics of the gilded coffeehouses. At a marble table, from heavy porcelain — never hurried.
items.tag: In a historic kávéház · at a marble table

items.name: Kürtőskalács — the chimney cake
items.description: A sugared cylinder of dough roasted on a spit: crisp while hot, its smell holding the whole street. Cinnamon is the classic, walnut the generous option — in winter it doubles as a hand-warmer.
items.tag: Hot on the street · cinnamon classic

items.name: Tokaji, kékfrankos and unicum
items.description: Sweet Tokaji has carried the title 'king of wines' for centuries; kékfrankos is the local pride of the table reds. The courage test is unicum, the bitter liqueur of forty herbs — the first sip is a shock, the second a habit.

callout.label: Market tip
callout.text: In the Great Market Hall (Nagyvásárcsarnok) the ground floor is for shopping and the upper floor for lángos and gulyás stands: go before the midday crowd, buy paprika and salami below, eat above. All of Hungarian cooking in one building.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the Parliament; these six are Budapest's steam-veiled backstage.

items.rarity: A night swim under a dome
items.name: Rudas — the rooftop pool and the Ottoman dome
items.description: After swimming beneath a 500-year-old Ottoman dome, climb to the rooftop hot pool: the Danube and Erzsébet Bridge at your feet. The Friday and Saturday night sessions are the city's best-kept programme.

items.name: The tomb of Gül Baba
items.description: An Ottoman dervish's tomb on the Rózsadomb slope: a rose-garden terrace with a Danube view, the saint's sarcophagus within. One of Europe's northernmost Islamic pilgrimage sites — and one of the city's calmest corners.

items.name: Margaret Island's northern tip
items.description: Everyone stays near the fountain; the Japanese garden, the small animal park and the water tower at the island's north are almost always quiet. Rent a bike and ride it end to end.

items.name: The Párisi Udvar arcade
items.description: Art nouveau's jewel box: the old arcade with its stained-glass dome has been restored to its glory. A coffee in its café is an excuse to stare at the ceiling — the city's most ornate 'roof'.

items.rarity: A time tunnel beneath the boulevard
items.name: An Andrássy tour by the M1 metro
items.description: Hop on and off at the 1896 metro's porcelain-tiled stations: Opera, Oktogon, Hősök tere. Two metres underground, a hundred years back — a boulevard tour for the price of a ticket.

items.rarity: A quiet terrace over the Danube
items.name: The Philosophers' Garden — Gellért slope
items.description: Five minutes off Gellért Hill's main crowds, a silent sculpture garden opens: castle, Parliament and bridges in one frame, tourists almost none. The sunset's hidden box seat.

callout.label: Choosing your bath
callout.text: Pick your bath by temperament: Széchenyi is yellow-palaced and social, Gellért art nouveau and elegant, Rudas Ottoman and mystic, Veli Bej local and calm. The rule is the same in all — lock the phone in the locker and surrender to the steam.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Budapest is a friendly city, but the classic games run along the tourist strip; know these four and wander easy.

items.name: The taxi hailed off the street
items.description: Some cars flagged by hand run on a 'broken meter' and a tourist exchange rate; a short ride becomes a long bill.
items.instead: Call the taxi by app or official dispatcher; at the airport take the official rank. Public transport + your two feet already solve most routes.

items.name: The street exchange booths' 'no commission' game
items.description: Some booths on the tourist strip lure with the rate and cut with the small print; the 'zero commission' sign is half the story.
items.instead: Draw forints from an ATM (answer the DCC question with 'local currency') or pay by card. If you must exchange, check a comparison app and pick booths off the main drag.

items.name: The Váci utca menu trap
items.description: Some restaurants on the walking street are famous for priceless 'daily specials' and swollen service lines; the bill arrives with a surprise.
items.instead: Never order a special without a printed price, and check the service percentage on the menu. Two streets in, or on Ráday, the same cooking costs half.

items.name: The night-time 'friendly invitation' game
items.description: In some venues reached via warm invitations in the tourist quarter, drink prices turn out astronomical, and the bill dispute ends with security at the door.
items.instead: Build the night around ruin bars you chose yourself: prices on the wall, a mixed crowd, a genuine atmosphere. Keep the no-venue-change-by-invitation rule all night.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Budapest say yes to nothing without a written price: taxi, exchange, 'daily special'. The written-price culture is the norm in this city — whoever strays learns the reason from their wallet.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From castle to bath, a full day on both banks

steps.title: A castle morning
steps.description: Funicular up to Buda Castle: look across to Parliament from the Fisherman's Bastion turrets and see the Mátyás Church roof tiles in morning light — before the tour groups.

steps.title: The Chain Bridge and the basilica
steps.description: Cross the bridge on foot into Pest; climb to St Stephen's dome terrace or catch your breath at a square café.

steps.title: Lunch in the market hall
steps.description: Lángos or gulyás on the Great Market's upper floor; paprika and Tokaji shopping below — the gift list ends in one building.

steps.title: Széchenyi steam
steps.description: The M1 metro via Hősök tere to the baths: the hot-cold cycle in the yellow palace's outdoor pool, chess-watching allowed.

steps.title: Andrássy and a kávéház break
steps.description: Back along the boulevard: the Opera façade, the arcades, and Dobos torte + coffee in a historic coffeehouse — an imperial late afternoon.

steps.title: Night: lights and a ruin bar
steps.description: A lit-Parliament loop on tram 2, then a ruin bar night in District VII: old armchairs, odd objects, long conversation.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Buda, Pest and steam — three acts

steps.title: Classic Budapest
steps.description: The one-day flow above: castle, bridge, market, Széchenyi, ruin bar.

steps.title: Parliament and the Jewish Quarter
steps.description: The Parliament interior tour in the morning (book ahead) + a pause at the Shoes on the Danube memorial; the Great Synagogue and a quarter walk in the afternoon; dinner in the Gozsdu courtyard, then Rudas's rooftop pool at night.

steps.title: Island, hill and farewell
steps.description: A Margaret Island bike morning; Gellért Hill + the Philosophers' Garden panorama in the afternoon; a Danube night cruise in the evening — Parliament golden from the water; that is how you say goodbye.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Hungarian is Europe's loneliest language — like none of its neighbours; these five still open doors with a smile.

items.meaning: Hello / bye — friendly and multipurpose; say it and smile
Please / you're welcome — courtesy's key word
Cheers! (and bless you!) — hard to say, great in effect; fine with beer, by legend never with clinked beer glasses of old
'Delicious' — said after a spoon of gulyás, it opens the kitchen door

checklist.title: Budapest Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Egészségedre! You've lived both banks of the Danube!

items.label: Surrender to the steam in a thermal pool
items.sub: Széchenyi, Gellért or Rudas — two hours minimum

items.label: Cross the Chain Bridge on foot
items.sub: Once by day, once by night
